name: Kumon
line: Kumon repeats worksheet sets an instructor grades. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Kumon: Kumon repeats worksheet sets that an instructor grades. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Kumon's unit is the worksheet set: a child repeats each set until it is fast and accurate, and an instructor grades the work and decides what comes next [5][7][9]. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. Every answer, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. In Kumon, a placement test sets the start, staff grade the worksheets, and each level ends with an Achievement Test of speed and accuracy [5][7][8]. Work done at home is graded at the next class, or within about 24 hours on Kumon Connect [4][5].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Kumon the unit is the worksheet set. A new skill is learned from worked examples printed where it begins, with no lecture, and the instructor gives hints in class only when needed [5][6][11].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer, AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. Kumon instructors avoid giving the answer right away. The child finds which part of the answer is wrong and corrects only that part [5][6]. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect, 0.49, against 0.32 for the correct answer alone and 0.05 for marking right or wrong [15].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Kumon repeats the same worksheet set until the child is fast and accurate, sometimes even after a perfect score [2][9]. Later levels build on earlier ones. We found no scheduled return to earlier skills in the Kumon pages we read [7][9]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on a test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [16].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts as learned when the learner gets it right without help, more than once, and practice moves on. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In Kumon the instructor decides whether a child repeats a set or moves on, from accuracy and time against its Standard Completion Time [7][9]. A child starts on work that should feel quick and easy, on purpose [7].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. Kumon places a child at one point in a fixed sequence of worksheets, which runs from counting to calculus [1][7][10]. Its topic list does not name geometry or measurement [1].

rows.range: Age 3 through high school, ending in calculus [2][10]. The topic list does not name geometry or measurement [1].
rows.start: A placement test at the center. A child starts on work that should feel quick and easy, on purpose [7][8].
rows.teaching: No lectures [11]. Worked examples printed where a new skill begins, and instructor hints in class only when needed [5][6].
rows.next: The instructor decides, from a fixed sequence of worksheets, the child's accuracy, and time against a Standard Completion Time [6][7].
rows.mastery: A set is repeated until fast and accurate. Each level ends with an Achievement Test of speed and accuracy [8][9].
rows.review: Repetition of the same set until it is fast [2][9]. No scheduled return to earlier skills found in the pages we read [7].
rows.print: Standard paper worksheets, sent home for the days between classes [5][6]. Kumon Connect puts them on a tablet [4].
rows.adult: The instructor plans and grades. The parent brings the child to class twice a week and keeps the daily routine at home [1][5][7].
rows.reports: Worksheets studied and levels completed. On Kumon Connect, time and score for each worksheet [8].
rows.evidence: One independent randomized trial, in Bangladesh: large gains in calculation speed and accuracy [11]. In 2009 the What Works Clearinghouse found no study that met its standards [13].

theirs: Kumon Math is an after-school worksheet program from Kumon Institute of Education in Japan. It began in 1954, when Toru Kumon, a math teacher, wrote short daily assignments for his son [3]. In the United States, local centers run it for children from age 3 through high school [1][2].

A child goes to the center twice a week and does worksheets at home on the other days, up to about 30 minutes a day per subject [1][2]. In class the child works alone while the instructor watches, gives hints only when needed, and grades the sheets [5]. New skills are learned from worked examples printed on the sheets [6]. The child repeats each set until it is fast and accurate against a Standard Completion Time, and each level ends with an Achievement Test [7][8][9].
credit: A person watches the child work twice a week and adjusts the plan [5].
An independent randomized trial in Bangladesh found large gains in calculation speed and accuracy [11].
Fast, accurate calculation is a stated aim, and completion time guides each decision to repeat or advance [6][7][9].

theirs: Kumon's strongest evidence is a randomized trial in Bangladesh by Sawada, Mahmud, Seki and Kawarazaki, published in 2024 in Economic Development and Cultural Change [11]. Thirty-four non-formal primary schools in and near Dhaka were split at random, 17 to Kumon [11][12]. Students in grade 3 or 4 did one 30-minute Kumon session a day, six days a week, for eight months, with no homework. Teachers trained by Kumon supervised, and Kumon supplied the worksheets. The Japan Society for the Promotion of Science funded the study, and the authors say they ran it independently of Kumon [11].

Kumon students scored about 0.47 standard deviations higher on a timed calculation test and about 1.0 higher on a speeded test of simple items. The authors note that parts of these tests resemble the daily worksheets. On the national primary school exam 8 and 20 months later, the gain was about 0.23, though only about half the students sat it [11]. The trial was registered about two years after it ended [12].

In 2009 the What Works Clearinghouse identified five studies of Kumon and found none within its elementary school math review that met its standards. The two with an eligible design failed because there was only one unit of analysis in one or both conditions [13]. We found no entry for Kumon in Evidence for ESSA [14].
ours: Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect, 0.49, against 0.32 for the correct answer alone and 0.05 for marking right or wrong [15]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on a test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [16]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: The goal is fast, accurate calculation, and your child does well with a fixed daily routine and a person who checks the work twice a week.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want every answer followed by the correct answer and the worked steps.
You want learned skills to keep coming back, mixed with other math.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You teach at home and want the program to place, check and review, with workbooks to print.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Kumon?
questions.answer: In Kumon a child repeats each worksheet set until it is fast and accurate, and an instructor grades the work and decides what comes next [5][7][9]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Kumon work?
questions.answer: For calculation, an independent randomized trial in Bangladesh found large gains in speed and accuracy and a smaller gain on a national exam [11]. In its 2009 review, the What Works Clearinghouse found no study of Kumon within its elementary math review that met its standards [13].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
